note: Auditable alert-to-action rules. Scopes: 'personal' rules are evaluated only while the detector has an open alert, so their false-alert rate is set by the detector's budget. 'vital', 'symptom', 'environment' and 'adaptation' rules bypass the detector: they react to a single entered value, a reported symptom or a cabin reading. u = mean deviation over the last three measured days, in robust standard deviations, in the direction of concern. Fixed thresholds are general clinical guidance or placeholders and need sign-off by a flight surgeon. A fixed rule looks at every reading taken on the most recent day that has one, so a later normal reading does not erase an abnormal one.

rules.title: Symptom that needs the medical officer now
rules.summary: You reported a symptom that should never wait for a trend. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Tell the crew medical officer now.
steps: Stop exercise and any demanding task.
Stay with another crew member.
If you are the medical officer, tell the commander: they are your backup.
The medical officer closes this in Keel with a note once it has been dealt with; until then it stays on your Today screen.
The medical officer leads care on board and decides whether to consult the flight surgeon. Keel sends nothing to the ground by itself: the daily summary carries only what you chose to share.
rules.tier_reason: Red-flag symptom. The medical officer leads care on board; the flight surgeon is consulted when a link exists.

rules.title: Fingertip oxygen reading is 92% or lower
rules.summary: The resting oxygen reading you entered is at or below the level at which general clinical guidance says to contact a clinician. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Tell the medical officer now.
steps: Repeat the reading once with a warm, still hand while someone fetches the medical officer.
Sit upright and rest.
Ask for the cabin oxygen, pressure and carbon dioxide readings.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend. Needs a second person now.

rules.title: Thermometer reading is 39.4 °C or higher
rules.summary: You entered a temperature of 39.4 °C or more. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Tell the medical officer now.
steps: No exercise.
Drink, rest, and repeat the reading in an hour.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Thermometer reading is in the fever range, or well above your usual
rules.summary: You entered a temperature of 38.0 °C or more, or at least 1.0 °C above your own earlier thermometer readings. Resting body temperature has been measured about 1 °C higher after two to three months in orbit, so the medical officer should judge a reading against your own earlier in-flight readings.
rules.action: No exercise today, and see the medical officer today.
steps: Repeat the reading in four hours and log symptoms at check-in.
Drink to your fluid target.
Keep some distance at meals and wipe shared surfaces.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Blood sugar reading is below 54 mg/dL
rules.summary: The reading you entered is in the range that general guidance says can cause unclear thinking or seizure. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Eat or drink something sugary now and tell the medical officer now.
steps: Stay with another crew member.
Repeat the reading in 15 minutes.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Blood sugar reading is between 54 and 69 mg/dL
rules.summary: The reading you entered is below the level general guidance calls low. For some lean, fit people a fasting value just under 70 can be normal; Keel cannot tell.
rules.action: Eat or drink something sugary, repeat the reading in 15 minutes, and tell the medical officer today.
steps: If you feel shaky, sweaty or confused, tell the medical officer now.
Do not exercise or do critical tasks until it is back above 70 and you feel normal.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Blood sugar reading is 300 mg/dL or higher
rules.summary: The reading you entered is far above the usual range. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Tell the medical officer now.
steps: Repeat the reading once with a clean fingertip.
Tell them about vomiting, great thirst or confusion.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold. Placeholder threshold for a clinician to set; not from a cited source.

rules.title: Blood sugar reading is 200 mg/dL or higher
rules.summary: The reading you entered is well above the usual range. One reading proves nothing.
rules.action: Repeat the reading before breakfast tomorrow and show both to the medical officer.
steps: Clean the fingertip and wipe away the first drop.
Note when you last ate.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Upper blood pressure reading is very low
rules.summary: You entered an upper reading below 80 mmHg, or below 90 with dizziness or fainting. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Stop what you are doing, hold on or strap in (lie flat with legs raised if you are under gravity), and tell the medical officer now.
steps: Stay with another crew member.
Repeat the reading in five minutes.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold. Placeholder threshold for a clinician to set; not from a cited source.

rules.title: Upper blood pressure reading is below 90 mmHg
rules.summary: The reading you entered is below the normal adult range. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Rest, drink, repeat the reading in ten minutes, and tell the medical officer today.
steps: If you also feel faint or dizzy, tell the medical officer now.
Change posture slowly, especially after a gravity change.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Blood pressure reading is 180 upper or 120 lower, or higher
rules.summary: You entered a very high upper reading. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Rest five minutes and repeat. If it is still that high, tell the medical officer today; with chest pain, severe headache or vision change, tell them now.
steps: Tell the medical officer now if you have a headache, chest pain, breathlessness or a vision change.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold. Placeholder threshold for a clinician to set; not from a cited source.

rules.title: Blood pressure reading is 140 upper or 90 lower, or higher
rules.summary: The reading you entered is above the normal adult range. A single high reading is common after effort, caffeine or stress.
rules.action: Rest quietly for five minutes, repeat the reading, and show both to the medical officer at your next conference.
steps: With a severe headache, chest pain or vision change, tell the medical officer now.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed reference value, not a trend.

rules.title: Heart rate reading at rest is extremely fast or slow
rules.summary: You entered a resting heart rate of 150 or more, or 35 or less. Keel does not interpret it. These two values are provisional and have not been reviewed by a flight surgeon.
rules.action: Stop, rest, and tell the medical officer now.
steps: Stay with another crew member.
Count your pulse by hand for a full minute to confirm the device.
Note the time, and any chest pain, breathlessness or light-headedness.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Resting heart rate of 120 or more
rules.summary: Your overnight resting heart rate, or one you entered at rest, was 120 or more. One such reading is enough for the medical officer to look. The value 120 is provisional and has not been reviewed by a flight surgeon.
rules.action: Rest for ten minutes, repeat the reading, and tell the medical officer today.
steps: No exercise until the medical officer has seen it.
Take your temperature and drink to your fluid target.
Note any chest pain, breathlessness or light-headedness: with any of them, tell the medical officer now.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold, not a trend.

rules.title: Resting heart rate above 100 on two nights
rules.summary: Your overnight resting heart rate has been above 100 beats per minute two nights running. Keel does not interpret it.
rules.action: Tell the medical officer today and take it easy until you have.
steps: Take a still two-minute reading with the chest strap.
Check fluids, temperature and how you slept.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed safety threshold (a common clinical convention, provisional, not reviewed by a clinician).

rules.title: Your mood has been very low for days
rules.summary: Your check-ins have been at the bottom of the scale for several days in a row. That is hard to carry alone on a long mission.
rules.action: Keel strongly recommends talking to the medical officer today.
steps: If you have thoughts of harming yourself, or cannot function, tell the medical officer or the commander now.
A private conference with the support team at home can be recorded and sent when a link opens.
You decide what is shared. The commander sees only that a conversation with the medical officer is advised, not why.
rules.tier_reason: Sustained very low mood should not wait for a trend.

rules.title: You reported a change in vision
rules.summary: Vision changes are common on long flights and have no proven countermeasure, so they should be recorded and reviewed.
rules.action: Tell the medical officer today.
steps: Now, not today, if it is sudden, in one eye, painful, or comes with a headache.
Cover one eye at a time and read the same line of text; note which eye and what changed.
rules.tier_reason: Needs to be recorded and reviewed.

rules.title: Vomiting after a high radiation dose
rules.summary: You reported vomiting within three days of a daily dose far above normal. Keel cannot tell whether the two are linked. How soon vomiting starts helps the medical officer judge the dose.
rules.action: Tell the medical officer now, and note the time the vomiting started.
steps: Sip fluids; do not take anything for nausea until the medical officer says so.
Tell the commander your personal dosimeter reading.
rules.tier_reason: Possible early effect of radiation: the medical officer leads, and consults the flight surgeon when a link is available.

rules.title: Radiation dose was far above normal over the last day
rules.summary: Your dosimeter's daily total is several times the mission's usual level, which is what a solar particle event leaves behind. Keel only sees daily totals, so it cannot warn you in time to shelter: the vehicle's radiation alarm does that.
rules.action: Confirm with the commander that the shelter procedure was followed, and report any nausea or vomiting.
steps: Keep your personal dosimeter on.
Log nausea, vomiting or unusual tiredness at check-in over the next two days.
Keel adds the dose to your mission total.
If you vomit, tell the medical officer at once and note the time: how soon it starts after the dose matters.
rules.tier_reason: Whole-crew exposure: the commander and the medical officer should both know.

rules.title: Throat or cough symptoms, and your readings are drifting
rules.summary: You reported a sore throat or cough, and your heart rate, HRV, skin temperature or oxygen has moved the way an infection would push it. Neither would trigger Keel alone; together they are worth acting on. Keel cannot tell you the cause.
rules.action: Take your temperature now. No exercise until you have. Tell the medical officer.
steps: Enter the thermometer reading below. At 38.0 °C or more, or with a cough or chest symptoms: no exercise today, and the medical officer decides what you do.
If you have no fever, no cough, no unusual tiredness or aches, and the medical officer agrees, a light session is reasonable. Repeat the temperature in four hours and log symptoms at check-in.
Drink to your fluid target and protect tonight's sleep period.
Keep some distance at meals and wipe shared surfaces until this clears.
rules.tier_reason: A symptom you reported, backed by your readings. Possible illness in a closed cabin affects the whole crew.

escalate.reason: Cough with falling oxygen: the medical officer should see you today, and now if you are short of breath.

rules.title: Body mass is 5% or more below pre-flight
rules.summary: Your latest body mass is at least 5% below your pre-flight level. Crews typically lose 3 to 4%; more than that deserves a look at food and fluids.
rules.action: Show the trend to the medical officer at your next conference and eat the full plan.
steps: Add a planned snack each day.
Check fluid intake: dehydration also lowers the reading.
rules.tier_reason: A cumulative change that a rolling personal baseline would get used to.

rules.title: The same symptom three days running
rules.summary: You reported a headache, vomiting, dizziness or a cough on each of the last three days. A symptom that does not go away deserves a look whatever your readings show.
rules.action: Tell the medical officer today.
steps: Say when it started, what makes it better or worse, and anything you have taken for it.
Keep logging it at check-in so the medical officer can see the course.
rules.tier_reason: A symptom lasting three days.

rules.title: You reported a rash or itchy skin
rules.summary: Skin problems are among the most common medical events on the space station.
rules.action: Show it to the medical officer at the next opportunity.
steps: Keep the area clean and dry; do not share towels.
Note any new soap, wipe or glove material.
A painful, blistering rash in a band on one side of the body should not wait: tell the medical officer today.
rules.tier_reason: Common and usually minor, but worth a look.

rules.title: Three nights in a row under five hours of sleep
rules.summary: Each of your last three nights was shorter than five hours. This is a fixed floor, checked whatever your own usual sleep is, because a personal baseline can make chronic short sleep look normal. The value is provisional: NASA schedules 8.5 hours and ISS crews average about six.
rules.action: Protect a full sleep period tonight, and tell the medical officer if tonight is short too.
steps: Ask the commander to move or drop a task if the schedule is the cause.
Dim the lights and stop screen work an hour before the sleep period.
Use buddy checks on critical tasks tomorrow.
rules.tier_reason: A fixed floor on sleep, not a trend.

escalate.reason: Five nights in a row under five hours: the medical officer can adjust the schedule or discuss a sleep aid.

rules.title: Cabin carbon dioxide is above 4 mmHg
rules.summary: The 24-hour average is at or above 4.0 mmHg, the limit ISS operations used from 2010 before lowering it to 3.0.
rules.action: Whole crew: check the air revitalization system now and move to the best-ventilated module.
steps: Commander or engineer: check scrubber status and fan airflow now.
Stop demanding exercise until the level is falling.
Anyone with a severe headache, confusion or breathlessness: tell the medical officer now.
Use buddy checks on every procedure until the level is back under 3.0.
rules.tier_reason: Crew-wide cabin issue: the commander or the engineer leads the fix, and everyone on board sees it.

rules.title: Cabin carbon dioxide is elevated
rules.summary: The 24-hour average is at or above 3.0 mmHg, the level ISS operations adopted after crews reported headaches and slips at higher levels.
rules.action: Check the air revitalization system and move work and sleep to a better ventilated spot.
steps: Commander or engineer: check scrubber status and fan airflow.
Avoid enclosed corners where air pools; raise local ventilation in sleep stations.
Log any headache at check-in so the link to air quality is visible.
Use buddy checks on procedures until the level is back down.
rules.tier_reason: Crew-wide cabin issue: the commander or the engineer leads the fix, and everyone on board sees it.

rules.title: Your headache may be linked to cabin air
rules.summary: Cabin carbon dioxide is above Keel's advisory line of 2.5 mmHg and you reported a headache. On the ISS, headache reports became more likely the higher the CO2 level went; an average under about 2.5 mmHg kept the risk very low. Keel cannot tell whether your headache is from the air.
rules.action: Move to a spot with better airflow and tell the commander the cabin reading.
steps: Log the headache at each check-in so the pattern is visible.
If it does not ease within a few hours in better air, tell the medical officer.
rules.tier_reason: Often eases with better airflow; the commander decides on scrubber checks.

rules.title: Nausea or dizziness soon after a gravity change
rules.summary: Common in most crew in the first two to three days after a gravity change. Keel cannot tell whether that is the cause: cabin air, low fluids and other problems can feel the same.
rules.action: Light duty today: slow head movements, small sips and snacks, and tell the medical officer before any suited work.
steps: Tell the medical officer today if you vomit more than twice, cannot keep fluids down, or have a headache with it. Medication is available.
Check the cabin carbon dioxide reading on the Today screen.
If it lasts beyond day 4, the medical officer should review it.
rules.tier_reason: Usually passes within a few days.

escalate.reason: Vomiting, or lasting longer than the usual two to three days.

rules.title: Your body looks like it is under strain
rules.summary: Resting heart rate is up together with other readings. This combination is often seen during an infection, usually once symptoms have started, but Keel cannot tell you the cause.
rules.action: Take your temperature now. No exercise until you have. Tell the medical officer.
steps: Enter the thermometer reading below. At 38.0 °C or more, or with a cough or chest symptoms: no exercise today, and the medical officer decides what you do.
If you have no fever, no cough, no unusual tiredness or aches, and the medical officer agrees, a light session is reasonable. Repeat the temperature in four hours and log symptoms at check-in.
Drink to your fluid target and protect tonight's sleep period.
Keep some distance at meals and wipe shared surfaces until this clears.
rules.tier_reason: Possible illness in a closed cabin affects the whole crew, and early rest is cheap.

escalate.reason: Strong temperature deviation, or this pattern has lasted four days: the medical officer should consult the flight surgeon when a link is available.

rules.title: Blood oxygen is below your normal
rules.summary: Your overnight blood oxygen has been lower than your own range.
rules.action: Take a fingertip reading now, sitting still with a warm hand.
steps: If the resting reading is 92% or lower, or you are short of breath, tell the medical officer now.
Check the cabin carbon dioxide reading. Keel does not show cabin oxygen or pressure; ask for them.
If the reading is normal, wear the sensor snugly tonight and compare tomorrow.
rules.tier_reason: Low oxygen readings need a second person to confirm.

rules.title: Your mood has been lower than usual
rules.summary: Your check-ins have been lower than your own normal for a while. That is common on long, isolated missions and easier to turn around early.
rules.action: Book a private conversation with the medical officer. You can also record a message for the support team at home; it goes when a link is available.
steps: Put one thing you enjoy and one contact with home on today's plan.
Keep exercise and the sleep period fixed; both lift mood, and short sleep makes low mood worse.
You control who sees this. Sharing it with the medical officer is one tap in Sharing.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, or cannot function, tell the medical officer or the commander now.
rules.tier_reason: Private by default; you decide whether to involve anyone.

escalate.reason: Lasting ten days or more: Keel recommends sharing it with the medical officer.

rules.title: Your sleep is short or has shifted
rules.summary: Your sleep has been shorter or later than your own normal for several days. Sleep debt builds quietly and shows up first as slower reactions.
rules.action: Protect a full 8.5-hour sleep period tonight.
steps: Switch your quarters to the warm pre-sleep light setting two hours before bed.
Last caffeine at least six hours before sleep.
If the schedule moved, use bright light after waking to bring your body clock along.
Keep safety-critical tasks out of your 1 to 7 AM low, or ask for a buddy check.
rules.tier_reason: Usually fixed by protecting sleep for a few nights.

escalate.reason: Reaction time is now affected or the pattern has lasted six days: the medical officer can adjust the schedule or discuss sleep aids.

rules.title: You are drinking less than usual
rules.summary: You are drinking clearly less than your own usual. A faster resting heart rate, headache or dizziness often follow, and Keel lists any of them it sees below.
rules.action: Drink one extra litre before the end of the day, spread over the next few hours.
steps: Aim for at least 2.0 to 2.5 litres a day and pale urine.
Log each drink bag at check-in so the trend is visible.
Tell the medical officer about any sharp side or back pain.
rules.tier_reason: Simple to correct yourself.

escalate.reason: Dizziness with low fluid intake, or no improvement after five days.

rules.title: Exercise has dropped below your plan
rules.summary: Your weekly exercise is well under your own normal. Without gravity, fitness, muscle and bone are only held by daily loading, and the loss is silent.
rules.action: Do today's session, even a shortened one, and plan the next three.
steps: If a device is down, use the substitute session: elastic bands, or the resistance device at a load it can still give.
If you are skipping because you feel unwell or low, say so at check-in so Keel can connect it.
Resting heart rate creeping up over the next weeks is the first sign of lost fitness.
rules.tier_reason: Getting back on plan is the countermeasure.

escalate.reason: Ten days below plan: the medical officer should adjust the prescription.

rules.title: You are eating less than planned
rules.summary: Food intake has been below your own normal. Under-eating in space speeds up loss of body mass, muscle and bone.
rules.action: Add one planned snack today and finish the main meals.
steps: Check body mass at the next scheduled measurement.
If food has lost its appeal or you feel nauseous, note it at check-in.
rules.tier_reason: Simple to correct yourself.

rules.title: Your reactions are slower than usual
rules.summary: Your reaction self-test is slower than your own normal without a clear sleep change.
rules.action: Repeat the test after a ten-minute break; if it is still slow, ask for a buddy check on critical tasks today.
steps: Check the cabin carbon dioxide reading on the Today screen.
Think about last night's sleep and today's workload.
rules.tier_reason: One slow test is common; a pattern matters.

rules.title: Resting heart rate or HRV is off your normal
rules.summary: Resting heart rate or heart rate variability has moved away from your own normal without another clear signal.
rules.action: Ease today's exercise intensity and check the basics: fluids, sleep, workload.
steps: Take a two-minute still reading with the chest strap tomorrow after waking.
If it has not returned to your range in four days, Keel will suggest involving the medical officer.
rules.tier_reason: Often explained by sleep, fluids or training load.

escalate.reason: Not back in range after four days.

rules.title: Several readings have drifted from your normal
rules.summary: No single reading stands out, but taken together your numbers are unusual for you.
rules.action: Do a full check-in today and repeat any reading that looks wrong.
steps: Check that the wearable is snug and charged.
If you feel fine and it clears in two days, no action is needed.
rules.tier_reason: A combined drift without a clear pattern.

escalate.reason: Persisting for five days without explanation.
